Author: @kenofken9458
Content:
This is a classic example of 19th Century thinking carrying over too far into the 20th Century. 

Giant artillery is a horribly inefficient way to do long range bombardment. Hugely expensive, with enormous crew requirements. It has to fire from a fixed position, so it's a sitting duck for air attacks. The barrel is blown out after only two or three hundred shots, and for all that a range of maybe 30 miles.

As the Germans worked out eventually, missiles are where it's at. Very high portability, hundreds of miles of range and plenty of destructive power.

I can only surmise that the lack of filmed visuals and artifacts of the rail gun were the reasons a TV segment was never produced.

Content:
It might have made a better shore battery. It's poor accuracy wouldn't matter because it would be shooting at moving targets anyway. The low rate of fire certainly was a drawback, but if the Allies didn't know that, it would serve as a deterrent against bringing ships close to shore for landings like D-Day or invasions of harbours.
Not sure if 47 km would shoot across the English Channel, but the Brits would have just moved anything valuable away from it's range anyway, I guess.
Biggest problem with Gustav was that it would be very vulnerable to carpet bombing, even with a smoke screen.

It also shows that bigger battleships would have been very impractical. The biggest guns (Yamato) had 18" barrels but a much faster rate of fire.

They totally devastated this very heavy fort and the damn communists had no choice but to give up. Another example is a smaller German railway gun near Ancio which was a major factor in keeping the Americans in place after they invaded Italy. These big guns just did the right job at the right time.
